priya.name: Dr. Priya Nair
priya.role: materials scientist (someone who studies what things are made of and how they behave)

case.title: The Duck Derby Flop
case.hook: Hi! I’m Dr. Priya Nair. I study what things are made of and how they behave, like how water, rope and air carry energy. My first case for you comes from the pond in Palmetto Springs. Last Saturday’s Duck Derby was a flop.

flyer.sub: 200 rubber ducks. One pond. First duck to the dock wins!
rows: Free ice cream for a year
flyer.foot: Every dollar helps the town library.

body: The wave machine made lovely waves for a whole hour. The ducks bobbed up and down, but NOT ONE reached the dock!
Next year I’ll rent the giant Wave-O-Matic 5000. Bigger waves will push the ducks to the dock. Right?

stills.alt: Hundreds of yellow rubber ducks floating on a narrow river in a city, with a long yellow float stretched across the water.

case.question: Will a bigger wave machine get the ducks to the dock? Why or why not?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: The wave went all the way around the stadium, but the fan in the red cap never left her seat. A wave is a pattern that travels. The stuff stays put.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: same wave, new stuff
clues.t: A wave can travel through a slinky, a rope, water, a line of kids or air. Every time, the tagged piece moved and came back to the same spot.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: measure the waves
clues.t: Amplitude is how tall a wave is, from the center line to a crest. The wave with the biggest amplitude carries the most energy.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: shake it yourself
clues.t: A hard wiggle made a taller wave with more energy. It knocked the cups down, but the red ribbon still only went up and down in its own spot.

solve.title: Will a bigger wave machine work?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Yes. Bigger waves push harder, so the ducks will float to the dock.
options.why: Check Clue 4. The taller wave had more energy, but the ribbon still stayed in its spot.

options.t: Yes, if the waves are longer. Longer waves go farther.
options.why: Check Clue 2. Every wave went the whole way, and every tagged piece still came back to its spot.

options.t: No. A bigger machine makes taller waves with more energy, so the ducks will bob higher. But waves carry energy, not ducks. The ducks will stay in place.
options.why: Case cracked! A wave carries energy through the water. The water, and the ducks floating on it, only move up and down as it passes.

options.t: No. Rubber ducks are too light for waves to move.
options.why: Check Clue 2. Heavy or light, every tagged piece came back to its spot. It isn’t about the duck.

crowd.afterText: keep your eye on the fan in the red cap.
crowd.title: Be the crowd

why.t: At big games, fans stand up and sit down one section after another. A wave of standing people races around the stadium.

todo: Tap Section 1 (or press Stand up!). Then tap each glowing section, in order.
Keep going all the way around. Wait too long, and the wave fizzles!
Keep your eye on the fan in the red cap.
crowd.alt: A model of stadium stands: three rows of fans in six numbered sections. One fan wears a red cap.
crowd.fizzle: The wave fizzled out! The next section waited too long. Start again at Section 1.
crowd.wrongSec: Not yet! The wave has to reach Section {n} first.
crowd.lapLine: The wave went all the way around the stadium!
crowd.q1: Where is the fan in the red cap now?

opts1.t: In her same seat: Section 2, seat 5
On the other side of the stadium
opts1.miss: Look at the red cap tracker. Did her seat change?

opts1.t: She went around with the wave
opts1.miss: Watch her when the wave passes. Does she leave her seat, or just stand up and sit down?

crowd.fact: Scientists timed real stadium waves. A wave races about 20 seats every second, but each fan only stands up and sits down.
crowd.q: So what traveled around the stadium?

opts.t: The pattern of standing up and sitting down: the wave

opts.miss: The fans stayed in their seats. What moved from section to section?
Seats are bolted down! What moved from section to section?

crowd.win: A wave is a pattern that travels. The fans (the stuff) just move up and down in their own seats. Clue 1!

swapwave.tagLine: Tagged! Now press Send a wave and watch your tagged {piece}.
swapwave.q1: Where is your tagged piece now?

opts1.miss: Watch the red tag. Did it ride all the way to the end, or come back?

swapwave.q: Which kinds of stuff can carry a wave?

opts.t: All five: a slinky, a rope, water, a line of kids and air

opts.miss: Look at your wave log. Did the wave go the whole way in the slinky and the air, too?

opts.t: Only things you can see wiggle
opts.miss: You can’t see air, but your log says the wave went through it. That’s how sound reaches your ear.

swapwave.win: A wave can travel through all kinds of stuff (mediums). Every time, the wave went the whole way and the tagged piece stayed in its spot. Clue 2!

duckloop.title: The duck’s secret loop
todo: Press Send waves across the pond.
Watch the duck, not the waves.
Look at the red path the duck draws.

why.q: What does the water really do?
why.t: Scientists who study water waves found that as a wave passes, each bit of water near the top moves in a small circle. A duck floating on top rides the same loop.

duckloop.loopWord: a little loop, back to the start
duckloop.done: Wow! The waves rolled 40 feet across the pond, but the duck only drew a little loop and ended up (almost) right where it started.

brackets.afterText: Now measure three waves on grid paper.
brackets.title: Measure the waves
todo: Tap two dots to lay a bracket between them. Or drag from one dot to the other.
Measure the amplitude, then the wavelength.
Do all three waves, then answer the question.

amp.name: Amplitude
amp.ask: Tap the dot on the center line under a crest. Then tap the crest above it.

wl.name: Wavelength
wl.ask: Tap one crest. Then tap the very next crest.

brackets.sqWord: Each box on the grid is 1 square.

miss.ampTall: That bracket goes from the top all the way to the bottom: twice too tall. Amplitude starts at the center line.
miss.ampSide: That bracket goes sideways. Amplitude goes straight up: from the center line to a crest.
miss.amp: Start on the center line, right under a crest, and go straight up to the crest.
miss.wlTwo: That is more than one wave. Go from one crest to the very NEXT crest.
miss.wlHalf: That is only half a wave. Go from one crest to the NEXT crest.
miss.wl: Wavelength goes sideways along the wave: from one crest to the next crest.
miss.energyWl: The swell has the longest wavelength, but wavelength is spacing, not height. Energy goes with amplitude.
miss.energy: Look at the amplitude column. Which wave is tallest?

brackets.q: Which wave carries the MOST energy?
brackets.win: Amplitude is how tall a wave is, from the center line to a crest. The tallest wave carries the most energy. Clue 3!

shake.afterText: Watch the ribbon and the cups.
shake.title: Shake it yourself
todo: Drag the hand up and down, or press Gentle wiggle.
Watch the red ribbon’s path and the cups.
Then make a hard wiggle and compare.

why.t: Scientists use a slinky as a model of a wave. You can see every coil, so you can watch what moves and what stays.

gentle: Went up and down a little. Stayed in its spot.
hard: Went up and down more. Stayed in its spot.

shake.q: What did the HARD wiggle change?

opts.t: It made a taller wave (bigger amplitude) with more energy. The ribbon still stayed in its spot.
The ribbon rode the wave down to the cups.
opts.miss: Look at the ribbon’s red path. Did it move toward the cups, or only up and down?

opts.t: Nothing. Both waves were the same.
opts.miss: Look at your log. Which wiggle knocked the cups down?

shake.win: A taller wave (bigger amplitude) carries more energy: enough to knock the cups down. But the ribbon still only went up and down. Clue 4!

rivertwist.title: What really moves the ducks?
todo: Press Race the ducks.
Compare the pond and the river.
Then answer the question.
rivertwist.pondLabel: The pond, with the wave machine
rivertwist.riverLabel: A river, where the water flows

photo.alt: Hundreds of yellow rubber ducks floating on a narrow river in a city, with a long yellow float stretched across the water.
photo.cap: A real charity duck race on the Pétrusse river in Luxembourg, 2017. The river’s moving water carries the ducks to the finish. Photo: Bdx, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

rivertwist.q: What really carries the ducks to the finish in a real duck race?

opts.miss: Look at the pond: big or small, waves only bob the ducks. What is different about the river?
Rubber ducks can’t swim! What is the river water doing?

rivertwist.line: Most real duck races float on rivers or streams. The flowing water (the current) carries the ducks downstream. A wave only passes through the water.
rivertwist.win: Twist solved! Waves carry energy. Moving water carries ducks.

raceplan.title: Mr. Ortiz’s new race plan
todo: Tap the right choice on each line to circle it.
A wrong choice gets crossed out.
Then stamp the plan.
raceplan.head: Duck Derby · Plan for Next Year
raceplan.sub: Palmetto Springs · Mr. Ortiz, with help from Dr. Nair

opts.miss: Bigger waves only make the ducks bob higher. Waves carry energy, not ducks.
On still water, nothing carries the ducks along. Where does water flow?

opts.t: Palmetto Creek, where the water flows
A wave carries energy, not ducks. Flowing water carries ducks.

opts.miss: Remember the cups and the ribbon: a taller wave has more energy, but the ribbon stayed in its spot.

raceplan.win: Next year’s Duck Derby will really race. Thanks, scientist!

tool.name: Tuning fork
tool.teaser: Strike two tuning forks, hear their notes and watch them vibrate in slow motion.
tool.done: You made sound from vibrations. A tuning fork sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: A metal fork that rings one exact note when you tap it. Musicians use it to tune instruments, and scientists use it to study sound.

tuningfork.title: Fast or slow vibrations?
todo: Strike each fork and listen.
Watch the prongs wiggle in slow motion.
Answer the question. Then dip a ringing fork in water.
tuningfork.wigTpl: In slow motion: {n} wiggles every second. For real: {hz} every second!
tuningfork.needBoth: Now strike the other fork. Listen: is it higher or lower?
tuningfork.model: A model: the prongs move in slow motion (128 times slower than real).

q.q: The high fork makes a higher sound. How do its prongs move?

opts.t: Faster: fast vibrations make a high pitch.

opts.miss: Count the slow-motion wiggles for each fork. Which one wiggles more each second?
Look at the numbers under each fork. Are they the same?

tuningfork.dipBtn: 💧 Dip a ringing fork in water

q1.B: Leaves can’t swim! Think about the duck: what moved across the pond?

q2.A: Think about the measuring game. Wavelength is the spacing. Which one is the HEIGHT?
q2.C: Color isn’t part of a wave here. Which measurement tells how tall a wave is?

q3.B: Think about the red tag on the slinky. Did it slide to the end?
q3.C: Something DID travel down the slinky. What reached the other end?

cer-4.label: your reasoning
cer-4.re: because|so |this shows|that shows|this means|that means|which means|proves|since

ans-2: Amplitude is how tall a wave is. Taller means more energy.
Try: The ___ carries more energy because its amplitude is ___.
ans-3: What happened to the red tag, the duck or the fan in the red cap?
Think of a test your friend could watch, like a floating leaf or a ribbon on a slinky.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this tell what travels, what stays, or how much energy a wave has?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A wave carries energy across the pond, but the water stays in place.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “wave”, “energy” and “stays”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
